statement:
Two sequences are defined by $a_1=1$ and $b_1=2$ and, for $n\ge1$,
$$a_{n+1}=a_n+2b_n, \qquad b_{n+1}=2a_n+5b_n.$$

Prove by induction that, for all $n\ge1$,
$$a_n^2+2a_nb_n-b_n^2=1. \tag{$*$}$$

(i) Let $c_n=\dfrac{a_n}{b_n}$. Show that $b_n\ge2\times5^{n-1}$ and use ($*$) to show that $c_n\to\sqrt2-1$ as $n\to\infty$.

(ii) Show also that $c_n>\sqrt2-1$ and hence that $\dfrac{2}{c_n+1}<\sqrt2<c_n+1$.

Deduce that $\dfrac{140}{99}<\sqrt2<\dfrac{99}{70}$.
solution:
**Induction.** Base: $a_1^2+2a_1b_1-b_1^2=1+4-4=1$. Inductive step: assume $a_n^2+2a_nb_n-b_n^2=1$. Then
$$a_{n+1}^2+2a_{n+1}b_{n+1}-b_{n+1}^2=(a_n+2b_n)^2+2(a_n+2b_n)(2a_n+5b_n)-(2a_n+5b_n)^2.$$
Expanding and collecting (the coefficients of $a_n^2$, $a_nb_n$, $b_n^2$ are $1+4-4$, $4+18-20$, $4+20-25$ respectively, i.e. $1,2,-1$), this equals $a_n^2+2a_nb_n-b_n^2=1$. So ($*$) holds for all $n$.

(i) Since $b_{n+1}=2a_n+5b_n\ge5b_n$ (as $a_n>0$), we have $b_n\ge5^{n-1}b_1=2\cdot5^{n-1}\to\infty$.

Dividing ($*$) by $b_n^2$:
$$c_n^2+2c_n-1=\frac{1}{b_n^2}.$$
As $n\to\infty$, $b_n\to\infty$, so $c_n^2+2c_n-1\to0$. Since $c_n>0$, the limit satisfies $c^2+2c-1=0$, giving $c=-1+\sqrt2=\sqrt2-1$.

(ii) From $c_n^2+2c_n-1=\tfrac1{b_n^2}>0$, we have $c_n^2+2c_n-1>0$, so (as $c_n>0$) $c_n>-1+\sqrt2=\sqrt2-1$.

Since $c_n>\sqrt2-1$, we have $c_n+1>\sqrt2$. Also $\dfrac{2}{c_n+1}<\sqrt2$ follows from $(c_n+1)\sqrt2>2$, equivalently $c_n+1>\sqrt2$, which is what we just showed. Hence
$$\frac{2}{c_n+1}<\sqrt2<c_n+1.$$

Taking $n=3$: $a_2=5,b_2=12$; $a_3=29,b_3=70$; so $c_3=\tfrac{29}{70}$. Then $c_3+1=\tfrac{99}{70}$ and $\tfrac{2}{c_3+1}=\tfrac{2}{99/70}=\tfrac{140}{99}$. Therefore
$$\frac{140}{99}<\sqrt2<\frac{99}{70}.$$
hints: Prove (*) by induction; the algebra collects cleanly.
Divide (*) by b_n² to relate c_n to 1/b_n².
Use b_n → ∞ to find the limit, and n=3 for the explicit bounds.
